objectives: Explain why rotating a signing key invalidates forged and stolen tokens
Change FUXA's signing key without breaking its configuration file
Describe what makes a signing key strong and how to keep it secret
Name the attack a new key does not stop and the control that does
takeaways: Rotating the signing key makes every token signed with the old key worthless, forged or real.
A key must be long and random, because a captured token lets attackers guess it offline.
Configuration files can be programs: check that the file still loads before restarting a service.
Anyone who can read the file that holds the key can forge tokens again.
A new key stops forged tokens, not flaws in the server's own code: FUXA 1.2.6 still hands out admin tokens through its token refresh, so limit who can reach the HMI.

checkpoints.question: You saved a new key in settings.js. Why does your old forged token still work?
options: FUXA has not been restarted yet
The key must be entered twice
Forged tokens never expire
The browser cached the old key
checkpoints.explanation: FUXA reads settings.js once, at start-up, and keeps checking tokens with the key it loaded then. Only a restart makes it load the new key. The browser never sees the key at all.

quiz.question: After the key rotation, what happens to the operators who were logged in?
options: Nothing, their sessions continue
They must log in again
Their passwords are reset
They lose their user accounts
quiz.explanation: Their tokens were signed with the old key and fail the check now. Accounts and passwords are untouched, so a new login gives them a token signed with the new key. That is why a rotation should be announced.

quiz.question: Which new key best resists an attacker who captured one token?
options: frangoteam752
CybICS-HMI-key
48 random hex characters
the admin password
quiz.explanation: Offline guessing tries variations of known defaults, names and passwords first. A long random key is outside any such list. Reusing the admin password would also tie two secrets together, so one leak opens both.

quiz.question: You remove the comment marks in front of the example key line and restart FUXA. The HMI disappears. Why?
options: The example key is blocked by FUXA
The entry before it lacks a comma, so the file no longer loads
FUXA needs a new password first
Comment lines cannot be changed
quiz.explanation: settings.js is a JavaScript object literal; entries need commas between them, and the last active entry has none. The syntax error makes FUXA exit at start-up, and Docker restarts it in a loop. Restore the backup, and add the key as the first entry instead.

quiz.question: In the virtual lab, which of these undo your new key?
options: docker restart of the FUXA container
Recreating the FUXA container from its image
Updating CybICS so FUXA starts from a new image
Logging out of the HMI
quiz.explanation: The key lives in the container's own file system. A restart keeps that file system, a recreate or an update starts from the image again with the default settings. Logging out only drops your token.

quiz.question: The check passed. Which risks remain?
options: Tokens signed with the old default key
Someone who reads settings.js forging tokens
Any client that reaches port 1881 asking FUXA's token refresh for an administrator token
Common words as signing keys
quiz.explanation: The check proves the default and guessable keys are refused. The new key is still only as secret as the file that holds it. And FUXA 1.2.6 signs a refreshed token for whatever user the client names when the old token is invalid, with the new key; only limiting who reaches port 1881, or a FUXA fix, closes that.
